note: Belacqua and the other lazy souls of Canto 4, still sitting in the shade of their rock.
The poets are climbing with the sun on their right, so Dante's shadow falls to his left. Virgil, ahead of him, casts none.
One of the poem's most quoted lines: "Vien dietro a me, e lascia dir le genti". Karl Marx adapted it as the motto that ends his preface to Capital.
Another line that became a proverb in Italian. The rebuke seems harsh for a glance over the shoulder, but the fault is the one this part of the mountain is about: letting anything delay the climb.
A blush of shame. Being ashamed of a fault is the start of mending it.

context: The poets are still below the gate. The souls coming toward them are the third group of the late repentant: people who died by violence and turned to God only as they died.

note: Psalm 51, which begins in Latin "Miserere mei, Deus": have mercy on me, O God. It is King David's prayer of repentance after his adultery with Bathsheba, and the Church's chief psalm of penitence. The souls sing it in turn, half the group answering the other.

quote: sunlight couldn't pass through my body
note: The sign that Dante is alive. His body stops the light and throws a shadow on the ground. The shades, made of air, let the light through.
The psalm breaks off in the middle. These souls are easily distracted, as they were in life. They left repentance to the last second.
Dante will go back to the living, and can ask their families to pray for them. Prayers from earth shorten the wait here, as Manfred explained in Canto 3.
Shooting stars at nightfall, and lightning flashing through the clouds of a late summer evening. Medieval science, following Aristotle, explained both as dry vapors catching fire in the upper air.

They died in battle, by murder or by ambush, with no time for a priest or the sacraments. They move in a rush, as their lives ended in a rush. The three who speak tell little about their lives and a great deal about their last minutes.
They were sorry for their sins and they forgave their killers. The Lord's Prayer asks God to forgive us as we forgive others.
The peace of Heaven, which Dante is seeking on this journey through the worlds of the dead.

context: He never gives his name. He identifies himself by his town, Fano, and by the man who had him killed.

note: The March of Ancona, the region now called the Marche, on the Adriatic coast. Romagna lies to its north. To its south lay the Kingdom of Naples, ruled in 1300 by Charles II of Anjou.
A town on the Adriatic coast of the Marche, the speaker's home.

quote: the blood where my life resided
note: An old belief, found in the Bible, that the life of a creature is in its blood (Leviticus 17).

In the territory of Padua. Legend said Padua was founded by Antenor, a Trojan prince. Medieval tradition also made Antenor the man who betrayed Troy to the Greeks, and Dante names the pit of traitors to their country Antenora after him (Inferno 32). The name hints that the Paduans had a hand in the murder.

Azzo VIII of Este, lord of Ferrara, who died in 1308. Jacopo had opposed him while serving as chief magistrate of Bologna, and is said to have insulted him. Jacopo allows that Azzo had some cause for anger, but not for murder.
La Mira, a town on the Brenta canal between Padua and Venice, on firm ground and on the main road.
Oriago, a village near the edge of the Venetian lagoon, on the road from Venice to Padua. Jacopo was caught there in 1298 and ran the wrong way, into the marsh.

quote: a lake form from my veins
note: He watched himself bleed to death. Each of the three stories in this canto ends with the body: where it fell and what became of it.

context: His story answers his father's. In Inferno 27, Guido died absolved in advance by a pope, and a devil still took his soul. The son dies alone and unconfessed on a battlefield, and is saved.

note: His widow. Neither she nor any of his family prays for him, which is why he walks with his head down.

A plain in the upper Arno valley. On 11 June 1289 the Guelphs of Florence defeated the Ghibellines of Arezzo there. Dante is thought to have fought in the Florentine cavalry that day, on the side opposite Buonconte. His question is about a real mystery: the body was never found.
The upper valley of the Arno, in the mountains east of Florence.
A mountain stream that runs down into the Arno near the town of Bibbiena, a few miles from the battlefield.
The hermitage of Camaldoli, high in the Apennines, founded by Saint Romuald in the eleventh century.
Where the Archiano flows into the Arno and stops being the Archiano.
His last word was a call to the Virgin Mary. In Dante's poem that one word, meant with the whole heart, is enough to save him.

An angel and a devil disputing over a soul at the moment of death was a common scene in medieval preaching and art. In Inferno 27, Saint Francis came for Guido, Buonconte's father, and the devil won. Here the devil loses.
A famous phrase, in Italian "una lagrimetta", a little tear. The devil speaks with contempt, but states Dante's teaching exactly: a single tear of true repentance outweighs a lifetime of sin.
The body. Having lost the soul, the devil takes out his spite on the corpse.
The account of rain that Dante's age took from Aristotle: moist vapor rises from the earth, meets the cold upper air and turns back into water.

quote: the power his nature gave him
note: Devils are fallen angels, and theologians held that they kept an angel's natural powers, among them the power to stir up winds and storms. Saint Paul calls the devil the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:2).
The mountain ridge that closes the Casentino on the west. The "great ridge" is the main chain of the Apennines, on the east. The storm fills the whole valley between them.
The Arno, the chief river of Tuscany. A river that runs all the way to the sea was called royal.
Dying, he folded his arms on his chest in the form of a cross, a last sign of repentance. The flood undoes the gesture, but too late to matter: the soul is already gone.
Of all the souls who ask Dante for something, she alone thinks first of his tiredness. Her speech is six lines in the Italian, and is among the best loved in the poem.

context: She asks only to be remembered. She names no killer and tells no story, and leaves the rest to the one who knows.

quote: Siena made me; the Maremma unmade me
note: A whole life in one line, like the words on a tombstone: "Siena mi fé, disfecemi Maremma". She was born in Siena. She died in the Maremma, the marshy, fever-ridden coastland of southern Tuscany.
Her husband. She doesn't accuse him in so many words. She says only that the man who gave her his ring knows how she died.
